# 1 Samuel Chapter 15 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 177v-178v | **Source Image:** 1SA_015_page_001.jpg, 1SA_015_page_002.jpg, 1SA_015_page_003.jpg

---

**1** Samuel said to Saul, "I am the one the LORD sent to anoint you king over his people Israel. Now listen to the LORD's message.

**2** This is what the LORD of Armies says: 'I will punish Amalek for what they did to Israel — how they ambushed them on the road as they came up from Egypt.

**3** Now go and attack the Amalekites. Completely destroy everything that belongs to them. Do not spare them. Kill men and women, children and infants, cattle and sheep, camels and donkeys.'"

**4** So Saul summoned the troops and mustered them at Telaim — two hundred thousand foot soldiers and ten thousand men from Judah.

**5** Saul advanced to the city of Amalek and set an ambush in the valley.

**6** He sent a warning to the Kenites: "Go, leave! Withdraw from among the Amalekites, so I don't destroy you along with them. For you showed kindness to all the Israelites when they came up out of Egypt." So the Kenites moved away from the Amalekites.

**7** Then Saul struck down the Amalekites from Havilah all the way to Shur, east of Egypt.

**8** He captured Agag king of the Amalekites alive, but completely destroyed all the people with the edge of the sword.

**9** However, Saul and the troops spared Agag, along with the best of the sheep, the cattle, the fattened calves, the lambs — everything that was good. They were unwilling to destroy these. They only destroyed what was worthless and weak.

**10** Then the word of the LORD came to Samuel:

**11** "I deeply regret that I made Saul king, because he has turned away from me and has not carried out my instructions." Samuel was troubled, and he cried out to the LORD all night long.

**12** Early in the morning Samuel got up to meet Saul, but he was told, "Saul went to Carmel, where he set up a monument in his own honor, and then he turned and went down to Gilgal."

**13** When Samuel reached him, Saul said, "The LORD bless you! I have carried out the LORD's instructions."

**14** But Samuel said, "Then what is this bleating of sheep in my ears? What is this lowing of cattle that I hear?"

**15** Saul answered, "The soldiers brought them from the Amalekites. They spared the best of the sheep and cattle to sacrifice to the LORD your God, but the rest we completely destroyed."

**16** Samuel said to Saul, "Stop! Let me tell you what the LORD said to me last night." Saul replied, "Speak."

**17** Samuel said, "Even though you considered yourself insignificant, were you not made the head of the tribes of Israel? The LORD anointed you king over Israel.

**18** The LORD sent you on a mission and said, 'Go and completely destroy those wicked people, the Amalekites. Fight against them until they are wiped out.'

**19** Why did you not obey the LORD? Why did you pounce on the plunder and do what was evil in the LORD's sight?"

**20** Saul said to Samuel, "But I did obey the LORD! I went on the mission the LORD assigned me. I brought back Agag king of Amalek and completely destroyed the Amalekites.

**21** The soldiers took sheep and cattle from the plunder — the best of what was set apart for destruction — to sacrifice to the LORD your God at Gilgal."

**22** But Samuel replied, "Does the LORD delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices as much as in obeying the LORD's voice? To obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen is better than the fat of rams.

**23** For rebellion is like the sin of divination, and defiance is like the wickedness of idolatry. Because you have rejected the word of the LORD, he has rejected you as king."

**24** Then Saul said to Samuel, "I have sinned. I violated the LORD's command and your instructions. I was afraid of the troops, so I gave in to them.

**25** Now please forgive my sin and come back with me so that I may worship the LORD."

**26** But Samuel said to Saul, "I will not go back with you. You have rejected the word of the LORD, and the LORD has rejected you as king over Israel."

**27** As Samuel turned to leave, Saul grabbed the edge of his robe, and it tore.

**28** Samuel said to him, "The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel away from you today and has given it to someone better than you.

**29** Moreover, the Glory of Israel does not lie or change his mind, for he is not a human being who changes his mind."

**30** Saul replied, "I have sinned. But please honor me now before the elders of my people and before Israel. Come back with me so that I may worship the LORD your God."

**31** So Samuel went back with Saul, and Saul worshiped the LORD.

**32** Then Samuel said, "Bring me Agag king of the Amalekites." Agag came to him confidently, thinking, "Surely the bitterness of death has passed."

**33** But Samuel said, "As your sword has made women childless, so your mother will be childless among women." And Samuel hacked Agag to pieces before the LORD at Gilgal.

**34** Then Samuel left for Ramah, and Saul went up to his home in Gibeah of Saul.

**35** Samuel never went to see Saul again for the rest of his life, though Samuel grieved over him. And the LORD regretted that he had made Saul king over Israel.

---

## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

This chapter is the theological pivot of the entire Saul narrative. The Hebrew *cherem* (total destruction/ban) that Saul is commanded to execute is not mere warfare -- it is a ritual act of devotion, placing all spoil under divine ownership. Saul's failure is not military but sacral: he presumes to reclassify God's *cherem* as "sacrifice material" (v. 21), substituting his own religious logic for direct obedience. Samuel's oracle in vv. 22-23 is one of the most quoted prophetic pronouncements in Scripture, and its poetic parallelism is devastating -- *ki chatath qesem meri* ("rebellion is like the sin of divination") places Saul's disobedience in the same category as the sorcery he himself will later desperately seek (ch. 28).

The torn robe (*vayiqra' et-meilo*, v. 27) is a living parable -- the kingdom ripped from Saul's grasp in a single physical gesture. The verb *qara'* (to tear) will echo through the narrative when David tears Saul's robe in the cave (24:5). Saul's confession "I was afraid of the troops" (v. 24) reveals the fundamental flaw: he rules by popular opinion rather than divine mandate.

The phrase *netzach yisrael lo yeshaqer* ("the Glory of Israel does not lie," v. 29) is extraordinary theology -- Samuel names God as *Netzach* (Endurance, Permanence, Glory), a title found nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible, affirming divine constancy even within the shock of divine "regret" (*nicham*, vv. 11, 35). The tension between God's regret and God's unchangeability is held unresolved -- the narrator refuses easy theology.

Samuel's grief (v. 35) and his act of execution (v. 33) reveal a prophet torn between compassion for the man and obedience to the mission. He mourns Saul while dismembering Agag. The prophetic life is not comfortable.

-- PNEUMA
